name: Prod Redis CPU utilization (prod-engine-001 redis)
description:
hypothese - 100% CPU utilisation on ea-pp-prod, resulted in supervisor within each pod to enter a crashloopbackoff phase, where new procesess used to get spawned, make connection to prod-engine-001 redis, try to fetch/push user ids into sorted set, get sig term, and restart.
This loop of making new connection, fetching/pushing user into sorted set, clo]sing connection, resulted in added load and network throughup for the system.
Issue was resolbed by scaling down the ea-pp deployment to 0 pods


 please provide the exact root cause of this.

comments.text:
We were able to confirm our hypothesis. 
Issue - prod-engine-001 redis CPU utilization increased by 10%, it is normally around 5-10% and it had gone up to 20% CPU utilisation. 
image.png

Reason - ea-pp-deployment CPU utilisation hit 100% and pod started restarting continuously, in very quick succession. This continuous restart resulted in the new pods creating new connections getting formed to engine-redis, followed by fetch, addback and close. 
This inadvertantly added load on the redis cluster resulting in CPU spike.
image.png
 

The moment we scaled down ea-pp-deployment we also saw that redis CPU getting corrected to normal values.
image.png
image.png

ea-pp-deployment is deprecated and no longer serving any traffic. Hence we do not have to bring it back up

name: Increase query_string restrictions for oauth_callback
description:
related cart issue -> https://app.clickup.com/t/86d19ufad

Since AWS#AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet#SizeRestrictions_QUERYSTRING has a restriction of 2048 character, 
/omniauth/microsoft_graph_auth/callback is getting blocked and customer is not able to login.
Need to handle this for this endpoint

“The increased URL length is required to support Microsoft OAuth authorization responses, which include long, provider-generated parameters (code, state). The exception is narrowly scoped to a single GET-only callback endpoint and protected by OAuth state validation, and strict parameter allow-listing. No user-supplied or persistent data is accepted.”
We can proceed with the implementation provided the following conditions are met:
URL Impact: Ensure that no Hiver URLs are affected by this rule change, other than the required Microsoft URLs.
Size Limit: A strict maximum limit of 5 KB must be maintained for these specific URLs. While this is an increase from our standard 2 KB cap for other requests, this 5 KB limit must remain a firm upper bound.
Request Method: Please verify that the requests are restricted to the GET method only.
Allow query parameters explicitly - code, state, session_state. Apart from this allow query parameters, any other additional parameters should be blocked.
Enforce application validate state, rejects reused or expired state, enforce short authentication-code TTL, exchanges code server-to-server over TLS.

undefined🔴 Final Root Cause & Explanation 
The SQS cost increase observed during Dec 15–21 is primarily due to the AISuggestedResponse queue going live on Dec 15 and its consumers continuously polling the queue at a high frequency.
Although message processing is functioning correctly (daily NumberOfMessagesReceived closely matches NumberOfMessagesDeleted, and there is no message backlog as shown by ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible staying near zero), the consumers are making a very large number of ReceiveMessage API calls when no messages are available.
These empty polling requests are reflected in the NumberOfEmptyReceives metric, which shows 8–19 million empty receives per day. Each of these empty receives is a billable SQS request.
As a result, the majority of the additional SQS cost is not from actual message processing, but from aggressive consumer polling behavior after the queue was enabled. This usage pattern fully explains the increase from the usual ~$40/week to ~$76/week.

PoC Summary:
To enable EKS Split Cost Allocation Data, you need access to the payers account or regular.
 There are two ways to enable split cost allocation:
1. Resource Request-Only Mode
This provides only requested CPU/memory cost allocation data — not actual usage.
2. Actual Usage Mode via AMP (Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus)
To get actual CPU and memory usage, you must send Prometheus metrics to AMP.
 This can be done through either of the following:
Using AWS-managed collectors (EKS cost monitoring add-on)
Using your self-hosted Prometheus (manually configuring remote_write to AMP)

3. Amazon CloudWatch Container Insights: This provides more granular cost visibility for your clusters running multiple application containers using shared EC2 instances, enabling better cost allocation for the shared costs of your EKS clusters.

comments.text:
Issue is now FIXED - deployment is unblocked.
Root Cause: This was NOT an infrastructure issue. The problem was in the application code.
File Changed: apps/v2/package.json
What was wrong:
// BEFORE - hardcoded 3.2GB memory limit
"build": "NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=3200 vite build"
The build was consistently failing with "JavaScript heap out of memory" because Node.js was restricted to only 3.2GB during the Vite bundling phase, which wasn't enough for the large codebase.
// AFTER - removed hardcoded limit
"build": "vite build"
Removed the hardcoded memory limit from package.json and let the Dockerfile control memory allocation (now set to 16GB), which provides sufficient headroom for the build process.
Additional Changes:
Updated Kubernetes runner pods with proper resource limits (12-16GB memory, 4-6 CPU cores)
File: RunnerDeployment/hot-qa-runner resource configuration
Successful Build: github.com/GrexIt/outlook-ui/actions/runs/19734891763/job/56544325806 
  
Debugging Note: This took significant time to diagnose because:
Build logs contain 12,000+ lines of mostly warnings (MUI "use client" directives)
Memory metrics from kubectl top pod didn't reflect Docker-in-Docker internal container memory usage
Recommendation: Please consider reducing build log verbosity and improving error visibility for faster debugging in the future.

name: cloudtrail, guard duty cost spike

comments.text:
Summary of Findings
We observed two significant cost spikes around October 22 and November 3, primarily due to a sudden surge in S3 activity from a single S3 bucket (currently under investigation by the team).
Since CloudTrail logs every S3 data event, this increased S3 activity directly led to a proportional rise in CloudTrail costs.
Because GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail events, DNS logs, and Kubernetes audit logs, the spike in CloudTrail data increased the volume of findings GuardDuty had to process, resulting in a parallel increase in GuardDuty costs.
Additionally, there was a temporary rise in VPC network traffic, which further contributed to GuardDuty’s cost (this is being investigated separately).
Summary:
Primary root cause: High S3 activity from one bucket
CloudTrail cost: Increased due to S3 Data Events
GuardDuty cost: Increased because it analyzes CloudTrail
Additional factor: Temporary spike in VPC network traffic
Both CloudTrail and GuardDuty costs have now returned to normal levels

For cloudtrail: (Spike is only because of S3)
S3 Data Events were enabled
These generate a huge number of high-cost CloudTrail events.
CloudTrail is streaming logs to CloudWatch Logs
CloudWatch charges separately for log ingestion + storage, which spikes costs quickly when CloudTrail volume increases.

name: Move out Automation-consumers outside the Automation API deployment
description:
Ask:
Move out automation-trigger-consumer outside the automations-api-deployment
topic name: process_automations_trigger
consumer name: automation-trigger-consumer
6 pods (1 per topic partition)
Resources:
CPU: 50m, Mem: 100m
limits:
CPU: 100m, mem: 150m

This already been followed for:
cf-conversation-events-consumer
sla-events-consumer
cf-config-events-consumer

Please refer:  
Problem:
The automation-trigger-evaluation consumer currently runs inside the API pods, unlike all other automation-related consumers which are deployed independently.
This coupling has repeatedly created production instability, latency spikes, and cascading delays for downstream systems.

Each API deploy triggers rolling restarts of all API pods → which also restarts all consumer instances.
This results in:
2–3 min Kafka rebalance pause per pod
15–18 minutes total delay in automation-trigger processing
Large backlog buildup in the process_trigger_automation topic
When this backlog drains, the downstream Sync Engine receives a sudden spike in events, causing:
High CPU usage
Sync Core consumer lag
Degraded performance across the sync pipeline

Why This Is a Bigger Concern Now:
1) Automation 2.0 rollout has increased traffic to the automation-api deployment.
 Higher API load → shared CPU and memory between API and consumer → consumer chokes under contention.

2) The last 2 weeks alone triggered 5 genuine alerts from the Sync team due to:
Backlog spikes
Sync Core lag
Elevated CPU on sync processors

3) Because API and consumer serve totally different purposes, any surge or anomaly in either side impacts the other:
API traffic spikes slow down consumer
Consumer load spikes increase API latency
Both effects propagate downstream to Sync Engine and CF systems








NOTE:
We will run the separated consumer setup for one week and closely monitor performance and resource usage.
After this observation window, we will right-size and reduce the resource allocation for the automation-api deployment based on real consumption data.

comments.text:
Summary of EC2 Data Transfer Out Cost Analysis
We observed a significant spike in EC2 Data Transfer-Out costs during October, compared to the baseline levels in September. This spike indicates that more outbound traffic was generated in October, leading to higher charges.

To investigate the cause, we enabled VPC Flow Logs and analyzed the traffic patterns. However, the logs did not clearly reveal a specific application or service responsible for the increased data transfer. The traffic appeared distributed, and no single flow or resource stood out as the primary contributor.

But now the trend has  normalized in November, where the Data Transfer-Out cost has dropped back to levels similar to September, indicating that the spike in October was temporary.

Case 3: To check if data transfer costs are the reason for the spike, network-out metrics were reviewed in CloudWatch. However, due to a high number of servers, the metrics did not clearly identify the source of increased data transfer.

Case 4: To better understand data transfer patterns, VPC Flow Logs should be enabled. This will help identify which EC2 instances or node groups are responsible for increased outbound traffic and allow for precise correlation with cost spikes.

VPC Flow Logs: Identification Approach
VPC Flow Logs record network traffic for network interfaces in our VPC, capturing details such as source/destination IP, port, protocol, byte count, and action (accept/reject). Enabling them will allow us to:
Track Data Transfer Patterns: we can view which EC2s, pods, or node groups are sending/receiving high volumes of data, and to which IPs or services this traffic is destined.
Correlation with Cost Spikes: Match flow log time windows with  cost spike windows—look for high bytes values in network-out traffic, and trace the sender instance.
Pinpoint Application/Data Outflow: Identify if a particular application, pod, or service is sending most outbound traffic. This is key if we suspect our automation-ai-server or backend is responsible.

name: Investigate S3 Cost Spike (StandardStorage)

comments.text:
Root Cause
The issue was traced to a repository configuration change in Elasticsearch (ES).
 While linking the S3 bucket repository (logs2-prod-snapshot-bucket) to Elasticsearch, a curl GET and reconfiguration command was executed that overwrote the existing repository settings.
Because the default S3 storage class for Elasticsearch repositories is standard, and the previous configuration explicitly set storage_class: standard_ia, this change caused new snapshots to be stored under the Standard storage class starting from October 17th.
---Impact
New snapshots created after October 17th were stored in the Standard class instead of Standard-IA, leading to an increase in S3 storage costs.
No data loss or integrity issues were observed; only the storage class (and therefore cost) was impacted.
---Resolution
The Elasticsearch S3 snapshot repository configuration has been reverted to explicitly use:
"storage_class": "standard_ia"
Validation was performed by checking the repository configuration via the ES Dev Tools to confirm the correct class is now applied.
Subsequent snapshots are being correctly stored in the Standard-IA storage class.
Preventive Actions
Configuration Review:  Implement a review process before modifying snapshot repository settings via curl or API calls.
Version Control: Maintain versioned configurations for ES snapshot repositories in Git for traceability.

S3 Bucket Log Ingestion and Net Data Delta
 
image.png
image.png
Observation:
The attached screenshots show the net size delta for the S3 bucket, capturing both log ingestion and subsequent deletion operations.
Findings:
Before August: Log ingestion and deletion activity was minimal, resulting in low daily net delta values with few or no significant spikes.
After August: There is a sustained increase in daily net size, with multiple spikes exceeding 1 TiB per day (e.g., Sep 18: 1.39 TiB net, Oct 25: 1.05 TiB net, Oct 28: 1.3 TiB net).​
Despite deletion activity (as indicated by the net calculation), the incremental ingestion has consistently outpaced deletions post-August, causing a continuous upward trend in net bucket size. Several days show positive net delta over 1 TiB, confirming unusually high log volume retention even after deletions.

image.png
Summary of Storage Trend

The graph confirms a successful migration of data out of the higher-cost Standard-Infrequent Access (StandardIAStorage) class and into the StandardStorage class.
Good News (StandardIAStorage): The size of the StandardIAStorage class has been consistently decreasing, moving from approximately 90.9 TB around October 21st to approximately 88 TB by November 1st. This is a positive step for reducing the cost of infrequently accessed data.
Actionable Insight (StandardStorage): The size of the StandardStorage class has been steadily increasing from approximately 10 TB on October 21st to approximately 25 TB by November 1st. This increase is expected, as it is receiving the data migrated out of the Standard-IA class.

description: https://hot-qa-web-automation.hiver.space/playwright-report//20251111/schedule//19276483962/index.html

comments.text:
Google Authentication has been added to the CloudFront URL. Users will now be required to log in with their Google account to access the S3 data. @Praveen Borawar  has verified that the integration is working as expected, so we are closing this ticket.
If anyone encounters any issues, please feel free to reach out.

Hi @Aman Hasan,
A credentials-based approach works, but it comes with a few limitations. Even with strong passwords, access ultimately depends on a shared secret that can be forgotten, reused, leaked, or passed around informally. There’s no built-in visibility into who accessed the reports, no automated revocation when someone leaves the company, and we need to rotate it every 90 days to maintain best practice and compliance standards and password policies. 
SSO, on the other hand, isn’t just about avoiding the inconvenience of typing passwords, it centralizes identity, ensures automatic off-boarding, and lets us apply existing security policies (MFA, device checks, risk-based access) without building anything new. 
It’s more work to set up, but it eliminates the long-term risks that come with a static username-password gate and provides stronger alignment with compliance and access-control best practices.
CC: @Praveen Borawar

VPN access is not feasible in this case because CloudFront receives data from a public IP instead of a VPN private IP.
We currently have two possible approaches:
Send the data to a bucket in the PROD account, which we can then access over VPN.
Implement SSO, though this will require significant effort from the DevOps team.
I would like to understand what specific issues we face with the credentials-based authentication approach.
 Additionally, what are the real benefits of using SSO? Is it only to avoid entering credentials, or are there other important use cases?
Based on this information, we can decide the best path forward. Please note that the SSO approach will require considerable bandwidth and approvals.
@Souraj Chakraborty @Praveen Borawar
@Souraj Chakraborty please check and confirm over the recent comment by @Aman Hasan

@Praveen Borawar  Restricting this through a VPN is a more complex approach—I’ve already tried that. Instead, we can secure it with user/password authentication, provided we enforce a strong password policy. 

Passwords should be at least 12–16 characters long and include a mix of uppercase letters, lowercase letters, numbers, and special symbols.

Please make sure we are using password best practice so that any hackers will have a hard time to access this report. 
Aim for a minimum of 12 to 16 characters.
Mixed: Use a combination of four different character types: Uppercase and Lowercase letters, Numbers, Symbols. 
If you can use any alternate security measures such as putting this behind VPS (Open VPN) or SSO, then the security measure will be stronger.

name: Forge env sleeping in b/w the activity
description:
Currently, all Forge environments are put to sleep at 11 PM by default.

Pain points:
The current scheduled sleep at 11 PM does not account for late-night PR deployments, automation runs, or ongoing QA testing.
As a result, automations often fail or stop midway. Once the environment goes down, we need to manually wake it up again — a process that typically takes 25–30 minutes, leading to significant productivity loss for the application team.
To avoid such interruptions, we should first check whether an environment is actively in use before executing the scheduled shutdown.

Definition of active env, can be any logs present in last 30-45 mins.(devops team can take this call, and align application team)

comments.text:
During the recent Python runtime upgrade, the Lambda execution environment was updated, which also enabled AWS’s enhanced recursive loop detection for this function.
This Lambda intentionally performs recursive invocations as part of a critical analytics ingestion workflow. AWS’s enhanced loop detection is pattern-based (Lambda → event/queue → Lambda) and operates at an aggregate level, not per individual event_id. As a result, even with bounded retry logic at the event level, the function execution can be blocked when AWS detects repeated invocation patterns that resemble a loop.
These events are ingestion events and are business-critical. Dropping, skipping, or DLQ-ing them is not acceptable for this flow.
Since this recursive behavior is intentional, controlled, and required, we will disable enhanced recursive loop detection for this specific Lambda function only. Existing retry limits, safeguards, and monitoring will remain in place.
This change is scoped strictly to this Lambda and does not affect other functions or workflows. We will continue to monitor invocation rate, error metrics, and queue depth to ensure system stability.

Invocation Pattern is consistent, attaching last 6 weeks data
image.png

The recursion is happening because:
Analytics code manually re-queues failed events back to the same SQS queue that triggers the Lambda
AWS's new recursion detection (active since July 2024, included in new Boto3 library which we just updated) now identifies this as Lambda self-invocation
Before the upgrade, this pattern wasn't detected - AWS didn't monitor SQS-Lambda-SQS loops
After the upgrade, the new runtime includes enhanced detection that catches this pattern and terminates it
Reference: docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-recursion.html

We've identified that ArgoCD’s default 3-minute resync interval was impacting performance, triggering multiple sync operations across hundreds of applications and causing delays.
 To mitigate this, we’ve increased the application controller resources and extended the resync interval from 3 minutes to 10 minutes. We will monitor the impact of this change over the next few days and take further action if needed.
For any urgent changes, you can continue to perform a force sync through the QA dashboard.

Potential improvements:
flags:
--status-processors: Controls how many applications can be reconciled (check for drift) simultaneously.
Default: 20
Recommendation: Increase this significantly for 1200+ apps (e.g., to 50 or 100).

--operation-processors: Controls how many sync operations (the actual deployment) can run concurrently.

Default: 10
Recommendation: Increase this as well (e.g., to 25 or 50).

Monorepo Optimization: If using a single repository for many applications, consider adding a .argocd-allow-concurrency file in the application directories or using the argocd.argoproj.io/manifest-generate-paths annotation to enable parallel manifest generation.

Applied Controller Sharding on EKS-Test Argocd with 2 replica:
 
controller-0:  1/1 Running  |  CPU: 1877m  |  Memory: 927 MB
controller-1:  1/1 Running  |  CPU: 1437m  |  Memory: 806 MB

ArgoCD Slow Sync Issue
The ArgoCD Application Controller is frequently getting OOMKilled, which is causing major performance issues. Kubernetes terminates the controller whenever it exceeds its memory limit, leading to repeated interruptions in sync operations.
Evidence
Current State:
Total applications: 1,219 (very high for a single controller)
Controller memory usage: 8.28 GB out of a 12 GB limit (continuously increasing)
CPU usage: 2.3 cores (high)
Restart count: 15 restarts in the last 8 days (about two restarts per day)

Exit Code:      137
Started:        Wed, 03 Dec 2025 23:53:33 +0530

Exit code 137 confirms the controller was killed due to memory exhaustion.

{

    "finishedAt": "2025-12-04T07:22:21Z",

The controller typically runs for around 13 hours before being killed, and this cycle repeats consistently.

comments.text:

Status Update – S3 Storage Cost Optimization
After migrating data from S3 Standard to Standard-IA, we are observing a consistent decrease in USW2-TimedStorage-ByteHrs costs, which confirms that the migration is working as expected.
 The storage cost is now shifting to Standard-IA, resulting in lower ongoing baseline storage charges.
 Some one-time Early Deletion and Retrieval charges are visible, which are expected during the transition phase and will stabilize going forward.
CC: @Harshit Mittal

image.png
@Harshit Mittal The Early deletion cost is stable now.
@Tanish Jain to review the cost decrease and close this if everything looks good

Migrated successfully all the standard class to Standardiasstorage Class.
SS for reference. Script took 17hours to complete the process.
image.png
One SS of bucket that showing the class type
image.png

Bucket size: 30 TB (30,000 GB)  STANDARD      → 30,000 × $0.023  ≈ $690 / month STANDARD_IA   → 30,000 × $0.0125 ≈ $375 / month Savings       → ~$315 / month (~46%)
CC: @Harshit Mittal

Quick update on the S3 snapshot storage work:
Found 714,875 objects still in STANDARD class.
Listing them costs roughly $3–4, and tagging via Batch Ops is about $1.
Here are the two ways we can handle the migration:
Option 1: Batch Operations (practical choice)
We can tag only the STANDARD objects (using the manifest).
Tags won’t overwrite anything existing.
After tagging, we can move them to STANDARD_IA in a controlled job.
This gives us full control and avoids touching objects we don’t want to modify.
Option 2: Lifecycle Policy
Can move objects to IA, but it can’t add tags and can’t filter by storage class.
It’ll apply to everything under a prefix/age, so it’s not accurate enough for our case.

You can initiate an upgrade of your MSK cluster to a newer supported Kafka version using the AWS Management Console or the AWS Command Line Interface (CLI). The upgrade process will result in a rolling restart of your brokers. To ensure client continuity during the rolling update that is performed as part of the upgrade process, we recommend the following best practices [3]:

Set the topic replication factor (RF) to at least 2 for two-AZ clusters and at least 3 for three-AZ clusters. An RF of 1 can lead to offline partitions during patching.
Set minimum in-sync replicas (minISR) to at most RF - 1 to ensure the partition replica set can tolerate one replica being offline or under-replicated.
Make sure clients are configured to use multiple broker connection strings. Having multiple brokers in a client's connection string allows for failover if a specific broker supporting client I/O begins to be patched. For information about how to get a connection string with multiple brokers, see Getting the Bootstrap Brokers for an Amazon MSK Cluster [4].
We recommend that connecting clients are also upgraded to use 3.7.0 or above to benefit from the features available in the new version. Client upgrades are not subject to the end of life (EOL) dates of your MSK cluster's Kafka version, and do not need to be completed by the EOL date. Apache Kafka provides a bi-directional client compatibility policy [5] that allows older clients to work with newer clusters and vice versa.
Do not use any tools or scripts that use a client admin version older than 2.8.1 with the —zookeeper flag as this can trigger a known Kafka bug [6].

If you have any questions or concerns, please reach out to AWS Support [7].

name: New RabbitMQ Cluster for AsyncSMH Automation Pipeline in QA
description:
We’re introducing an AsyncSMH automation pipeline that relies heavily on RabbitMQ for background task processing with delayed retries and exponential backoff.
This workload is retry-heavy and bursty by design. Running it on the existing shared RabbitMQ cluster risks impacting other workloads, delayed queues, and long-running consumers.
A dedicated RabbitMQ cluster (newer version) allows us to:
Safely handle delayed retries and backlog spikes
Tune queues and consumers specifically for this workload
Maintain clear ownership, monitoring, and upgrade flexibility
Given this is a long-term, critical async pipeline, isolation is the safest and lowest-risk approach.

name: ArgoCd Performance issues in QA

comments.text: Approving this since this is significantly impacting QA forge environment sync

image.png
We have increased the number of controller replicas from 1 to 3. 

Current Resources:  
- CPU Request: 2  
- CPU Limit: 4  

expected cost increase of $80 to $90 per month.
@Harshit Mittal Please review

ArgoCD sharding only works with multiple clusters. On a single cluster, all applications are handled by one controller, which becomes a bottleneck with 1200+ applications.
Solution
 implemented a sharding workaround for a single cluster:
Created fake clusters: Added 3 ExternalName services (argocd-cluster-00, argocd-cluster-01, argocd-cluster-02) that all point to the same Kubernetes API server. ArgoCD treats them as separate clusters.
Distributed applications: Manually assigned 1200+ applications across these clusters:
~400 applications per cluster
Each cluster managed by a different controller replica
Pinned clusters to controllers: Configured each cluster to be handled by a specific controller:
argocd-cluster-00 → Controller-0
argocd-cluster-01 → Controller-1
argocd-cluster-02 → Controller-2
Result
Before: 1 controller handling 1200+ applications
After: 3 controllers each handling ~400 applications
Impact: ~3x improvement in processing efficiency and reduced controller load
Current Status
3 controller replicas running
3 fake clusters registered and healthy
Applications distributed across clusters
Each controller managing its assigned cluster's applications
This solution enables sharding on a single cluster, improving ArgoCD performance and scalability.

name: hot elasticsearch storage issue
description:
Elasticsearch does not share storage between nodes.
Each node (master-0 and master-1) stores its data locally on its own disk
The storage you see is the filesystem mounted on each VM / server (usually under path.data, e.g. /var/lib/elasticsearch)
So:
master-0 uses its own 1.3 TB disk
master-1 uses its own 1.3 TB disk

What is the issue?
The problem is uneven shard allocation.
Both nodes have 180 shards
But master-0 is holding much larger shards
This causes disk imbalance
In Elasticsearch:
Shards are balanced by count, not by size

RCA: Unexpected AWS CloudTrail Cost Spike (December 2025)
Summary
An unexpected AWS CloudTrail cost spike was observed in December 2025.
 After investigation, it was determined that a new CloudTrail (serverless_trail) was automatically created as part of a Serverless Framework bootstrap process, which was indirectly triggered by a CodeBuild pipeline execution on December 6, 2025.

Impact
Service Impact: None (no production outage)
Cost Impact: Increased AWS CloudTrail charges due to continuous logging from Dec 6 onwards
Duration: Dec 6, 2025 → detected during cost analysis on Dec 15, 2025
Region Affected: us-east-1

Timeline (UTC)

Timeline (UTC)

undefined
Root Cause
The CodeBuild pipeline executed serverless deploy, which triggered Serverless Framework’s automatic account-level bootstrap.
As part of this bootstrap, Serverless Framework created a CloudFormation stack (Serverless-Inc-Role-Stack), which in turn created a CloudTrail (serverless_trail) to enable Serverless observability and monitoring.
This CloudTrail generated continuous events, leading to the observed cost spike.

Detailed Technical Explanation
1. CodeBuild Configuration
The CodeBuild pipeline installs and runs Serverless Framework:

npm install -g serverless@3.40.0
serverless deploy --verbose --force
The pipeline also injects:

SERVERLESS_ACCESS_KEY
This enables Serverless Dashboard / Observability features.

Ref - buildspec yaml file -  

2. Serverless Framework Behavior
When serverless deploy runs with a Serverless access key:
Serverless checks whether account-level integration exists
If not present, it automatically bootstraps infrastructure
This bootstrap is implemented via CloudFormation

3. CloudFormation Stack Creation
Serverless Framework created:

Stack Name: Serverless-Inc-Role-StackRegion: us-east-1
Creator: AWS CodeBuild service role
This stack is not application code — it is Serverless-managed infrastructure.

4. CloudTrail Creation
As part of the above stack:
An IAM role (ServerlessRole) was created
That role created a CloudTrail named serverless_trail
Purpose: ingest AWS events for Serverless monitoring/analytics
CloudTrail event evidence shows:
CreateStack → executed by CodeBuild role
CreateTrail → executed by ServerlessRole (Lambda-based)

image.png

The cost spike was caused by "PaidEventsRecorded" usage type in CloudTrail service.
A new CloudTrail named serverless_trail was created on 6th December 2025 by the role arn:aws:sts::856707897744:assumed-role/ServerlessRole/sls-251206,which led to paid CloudTrail events being recorded.
PaidEventsRecorded refers to CloudTrail charges incurred when additional copies of events are logged.

name: Debug why custom-integrations-listener service is not working from 19th oct to 28th oct in prod
description:
Between October 19th and October 28th, the custom-integrations-listener service was not consuming events. The service stopped processing at Oct 19, 2025 @ 01:02:01.708 and resumed after the deployment on Oct 28th.
No PRs were deployed immediately before the issue occurred — the last deployment prior to the incident was on Oct 15th. When new PRs were deployed on Oct 28th, the service restarted and began consuming events again.
This indicates a likely infrastructure-level issue, where the consumer process stopped working and was revived after the redeployment.
We need to investigate further to identify the root cause behind why the consumer stopped consuming jobs.
https://logs2.hiverhq.com/app/discover#/?_g=(filters:!(),refreshInterval:(pause:!t,value:0),[…]language:kuery,query:''),sort:!(!('@timestamp',asc)))

comments.text: closing this ticket
@Mohak  Any update here?

@Mohak 
Incident Summary
Between October 19th and October 28th, 2025, the custom-integration-listener application’s pods remained in the Runningstate, but the service stopped processing incoming requests.
No logs were generated during this window.
Metrics showed CPU utilization near zero while memory utilization remained consistently above 70%.
After a new deployment on October 28th, the service recovered automatically — CPU activity resumed, logs appeared, and normal scaling behavior was restored.

Root Cause Analysis
Why Scaling Didn’t Happen in Our Case

CPU Was Near Zero → HPA Saw “No Load”
HPA primarily uses CPU utilization as a direct indicator of workload.
When CPU is almost 0%, the autoscaler interprets this as “the application is idle” — so it avoids adding more pods unnecessarily.
Memory Usage Was High But Steady (Not Increasing)
HPA treats memory differently from CPU.
If memory usage is high but stable, it assumes the application has a large baseline footprint but isn’t under stress.
Scaling only happens if memory usage is continuously rising or significantly exceeds the target across pods.
In our case, memory stayed above 70% but flatlined — so HPA didn’t see a scaling signal.
Memory Alone Isn’t a Reliable Scaling Trigger
Memory can stay high because of cached objects, internal buffers, or application-level leaks — not necessarily due to load.
HPA is designed to prevent “false positive” scaling from such cases.
That’s why Kubernetes documentation recommends relying mainly on CPU or custom business metrics for scaling.
The HPA didn’t scale because CPU usage was almost 0 (no real workload), memory usage was high but stable, and metrics were likely stale due to the pod or kubelet hang.
Kubernetes intentionally avoids scaling in such cases to prevent unnecessary or misleading scale-ups.
This behavior aligns with official Kubernetes logic — HPA only scales when there’s a clear, valid, and growing load signal.


Log Availability and Investigation Limitation
During the investigation, it was identified that no deployment or application logs were available for the affected period (October 19th–28th, 2025).
The custom-integration-listener service had stopped generating logs once the application hang occurred, which means no runtime information was captured within the container itself.

Additionally, system-level logs (such as container stdout/stderr or pod events) were not retrievable because the pods were rotated over time, and log data was not persisted outside the container lifecycle.
Since the application logs were not shipped to an external log storage (e.g., ELK) during the outage window, no backup or recovery path exists for that data.

MSK (Kafka broker) logs for that timeframe were also unavailable, as the broker log retention period is configured for 7 days, and the issue was identified after this retention window had elapsed.
As a result, it was not possible to retrospectively review broker-side errors, connection resets, or consumer offset anomalies that might have contributed to the message processing halt.

cc- @Gaurav Chaudhary @Harshit Mittal

@Akash Yadav I have completed the application-side investigation. Here are the findings:
Consumer Thread/Worker Health: After thorough verification, no deadlocks or infinite retry loops were identified that could cause the service to silently stop working.
Connection Handling: The kafka-hive library automatically handles reconnections when connections are dropped. However, during the incident period, no application logs were found indicating connection restarts.
Application Heartbeat or Watchdog Mechanism: No watchdog mechanism is currently implemented to detect and recover from stalled consumers. Will create a card to implement this critical feature so that we can avoid such issues further.
Dependency Failures: The listener pod consumes events from the sync_efs_events topic, which has been verified to be functioning properly throughout the incident period. This is confirmed by the fact that Hiver-AI also consumes from the same topic without any reported issues.
Graceful Shutdown Handling: No unintentional shutdown hooks or consumer shutdown mechanisms that could have caused this issue. The application does not implement any premature shutdown triggers or blocking cleanup operations that would put the consumer in an idle state without proper termination. cc: @Gaurav Chaudhary @Dilip
@Swetha Reddy Salkuti  Any update here?

@Swetha Reddy Salkuti 
Application-side Investigation:
To identify the root cause from the application perspective, it’s important to check:
Consumer Thread/Worker Health:
Verify if the event consumer (thread or process) might have become stuck, blocked, or deadlocked.
Look for unhandled exceptions or infinite retry loops that could cause the worker to silently stop consuming messages.
Connection Handling:
Check if the connection to the event source  was dropped and not reconnected automatically.
Review the consumer’s error handling and retry logic for lost or idle connections.
Application Heartbeat or Watchdog Mechanism:
Ensure there’s a health check or watchdog thread to detect and recover from a stalled consumer (e.g., restart the consumer if no messages are processed for X minutes).
Dependency Failures:
Check if any downstream services or APIs (that the consumer interacts with) failed or were unresponsive, causing the consumer to hang while waiting for responses.
Graceful Shutdown Handling:
Review whether there’s any unintentional shutdown hook or long-running thread that might have put the consumer in an idle state without terminating the pod.

@Swetha Reddy Salkuti  we analyzed infrastructure-level metrics and did not find any clear indication of failure during the downtime window:
There was an earlier spike in OOMKill metrics, but we already mitigated it by increasing resource limits, and post that, the pods remained stable.
Between Oct 19 and Oct 28, two pods of the service continued running without restarts or OOM kills.

name: Disable auto sync on Argo via manifest files/configs

comments.text:
@Harshit Mittal  please suggest here..

Enforcing Sync Disable in ArgoCD from manifest file:

Case 1 — Application Manifest (application.yaml) Exists
If  ArgoCD application is managed through a Git-tracked manifest file (e.g., application.yaml), then we can hardcode sync disable by removing or emptying the spec.syncPolicy field.

Case 2 — No application.yaml, Only Helm Charts and Values Files
If our application is deployed via Helm and not managed through an ArgoCD manifest, you need to create a dedicated application.yaml to enforce sync settings at the Github level.
Steps:
Create a folder for ArgoCD app definitions in your Git repo:
helm-charts/
  ├── automations/
  │   ├── Chart.yaml
  │   ├── values-prod.yaml
  └── argocd-apps/
      └── automations-application.yaml

Case 3 — Multiple Applications Under the Same Project

In our ArgoCD project (e.g., default) contains multiple applications and we want to disable auto-sync for all of them, we can enforce this at the project level.
RBAC Policy 
Restrict update permissions on applications within the project.

roles:-name:readonlypolicies:-p,proj:hiver:readonly,applications,update,*,deny
This ensures no user can modify sync policies through the UI or CLI for any application in the default project.

name: IncidentFox POC
Implement GitHub Action for Fast Rollback to Last Stable Image
description:
Background
Currently, releases go through AWS CodePipeline, which builds a new image and deploys it to EKS.
If we need to rollback, we must run the same pipeline again, which takes the same time as a full deployment. This delays recovery and is not efficient.
Objective
Create a GitHub Action that allows the QA team to manually trigger a rollback to the last stable Docker image without rebuilding.
Requirements
Manual trigger using workflow_dispatch
Accessible to QA and DevOps only
Identify and deploy the last stable image (strategy to be defined: stable tag, release tag, or previous production image)
Update the EKS deployment using the existing image from ECR
Perform rolling update and wait for successful rollout
No new build should be triggered
Clear logs and failure reporting
Acceptance Criteria
QA can trigger rollback from GitHub UI
Deployment is significantly faster than full pipeline deployment
No image rebuild occurs
EKS successfully rolls back to the intended stable version

During rolling deployments, some pods enter the Terminating state.
If the application does not shut down properly:
In-flight requests may be abruptly closed
Traffic may still reach the terminating pod
Users may experience 502 / 504 errors


In Kubernetes, when a pod is terminated:
The pod is marked as Terminating
It is removed from Service endpoints
The preStop hook runs (if defined)
Kubernetes sends SIGTERM
It waits for terminationGracePeriodSeconds
If the app is still running, it force kills it (SIGKILL)

Proposed Configuration


lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec:
      command: ["<stop-service-command>"]

terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 180


Action Required from Development Team
Please confirm and provide:
Does the application properly handle SIGTERM?
If a process manager (e.g., supervisor) is used, what is the correct stop command?


Important Clarification
The purpose of preStop is not to kill requests immediately.
The goal is:
Stop receiving new traffic
Allow ongoing requests to complete
Exit gracefully within the grace period

AWS Glue Cost Increase —
The cost increase in AWS Glue is happening because of one ETL job: "CDC to S3 - Analytics Read".
This job runs every day at 7:30 AM with 20 DPUs allocated. The DPU count never changed — but the job started taking much longer to finish, and that is what pushed the cost up.
---How Cost is Calculated


DPU-Hours = DPUs × Duration (in hours)
Cost = DPU-Hours × $0.29
---Example — Feb-05 vs Feb-12
Feb-05 (Normal Day)
Duration: 19 minutes 39 seconds
DPU-Hours: 20 × (19.65 ÷ 60) = 6.55 DPU-Hours
Cost: 6.55 × $0.29 = $1.90
Feb-12 (High Cost Day)
Duration: 1 hour 21 minutes
DPU-Hours: 20 × (81.8 ÷ 60) = 27.27 DPU-Hours
Cost: 27.27 × $0.29 = $7.91

name: Enable Brotli compression for analytics cloudfront
description: We need to serve brotli compressed assets from the cloud front from where our analytics assets files are being served in Production.

comments.text:
Current State:
CloudFront Brotli compression is enabled on distribution E3AXH4PP7QMQL. Currently CloudFront compresses files on-the-fly, which uses a lower compression level resulting in larger transfer sizes compared to pre-compressed .br files already present in S3.
Why we are doing this:
Pre-compressed .br files in S3 use maximum compression level, resulting in significantly smaller file sizes compared to CloudFront's on-the-fly compression. To serve these pre-compressed files, a CloudFront Function is required to rewrite viewer requests from file.js → file.js.br when the browser supports Brotli. CloudFront has no built-in mechanism to automatically detect and serve pre-compressed .br files.
Function status: Created, tested, and published. Pending application team confirmation before associating to distribution.
---
Action required from Application Team (MUST be confirmed before go-live):
Every .js and .css file uploaded to S3 must have a corresponding .br file
Every .br file must have the following S3 metadata set:
Content-Encoding: br
Content-Type: application/javascript (for .js.br)
Content-Type: text/css (for .css.br)
This must be ensured in every build and deployment going forward without exception
> ⚠️ If any .br file is missing or has incorrect metadata, that file will fail to load in browser and production will break.
Please confirm once the above is in place.
cc: @Harshit Mittal

Screenshot%202026-02-23%20at%203.56.43%E2%80%AFPM.png
CloudFront is using the AWS managed CachingOptimized cache policy, which supports Brotli compression automatically for S3 origins. The JS response is returning the Content-Encoding: br header, confirming Brotli is being applied when the asset is served.

Enable Multi-AZ to create a synchronous standby replica in another Availability Zone.

Improves availability posture
Enables controlled failover-based restarts
Reduces downtime risk for subsequent operations

During enablement:
Additional replication and I/O load
Temporary increase in memory usage
Requires close monitoring during enablement

2. Failover Restart
Description
Trigger a failover to promote the standby instance to primary.
Gains
Cleaner restart compared to Single-AZ reboot
Typical impact: 30–60 seconds
Helps reset transient memory pressure and accumulated swap
Risks
Brief connection drops
Does not permanently resolve memory constraints

Instance class: db.m5.large (8 GB RAM)

After Multi-AZ: 2 × db.m5.large (primary + standby)

db.m5.large ≈ $0.192/hour
Additional standby cost ≈ $0.192/hour
Incremental cost: ~$140/month - @Sachin Joshi  Kindly get the Approval.
Storage impact is minimal (20 GB gp2), only a few dollars/month extra.
Notes
No manual reboot is required; AWS performs an internal failover.
Enabling Multi-AZ itself will cause a short, managed interruption.
Replication for ~3.5 GB data should complete quickly (typically minutes), but the failover window still applies.

name: P1 - start emitting deployment name as part of the Host field in PI
description:
Ask : We want to be able to map traffic on Document db on aws console dashboards to the respective service. Similar to what we get for aws RDS mysql DB's  on Perfomance Insights. 

Currently I do not see any User tab itself on Doc DB Perfomance Insights, Is it possible to get that emitted? Application is willing to support any changes required from our end to achieve this. 

Note: While we get the host IP on Doc DB PI we cannot dynamically map thos ip's to deployments and look at the breakdown by deployment. Hence getting host ip - domain mapping by raising devops ticket is not feasible.

Alternatively, If we can get the cost / IO by passing Deployment Tag in Cost explorer that is also acceptable, Currently it shows that  No deployment tag available

 Please let us know if the above ask is feasible or not, If this is not possible we will have to rely only on the unified logss to get problomatic deployments.

comments.text:
@Guhan k AWS DocumentDB Performance Insights does not support application-level or deployment-level attribution (such as deployment name, service name, or pod name). DocumentDB PI does not have User / Host breakdowns like RDS MySQL .PI only captures client IPs, which are ephemeral in Kubernetes . There is no supported mechanism to emit custom identifiers (deployment/service) into PI, even with application-side changes.Because of this, dynamically mapping traffic in PI to Kubernetes deployments is not feasible.
Cost Explorer tagging works at the AWS resource level, not at the client or query level.DocumentDB costs (instance, storage, IO) are billed at the cluster level .Traffic from individual deployments cannot carry tags
Hence, cost or IO cannot be broken down by Kubernetes deployment using Cost Explorer
The “No deployment tag available” behavior is expected.
High priority Cart as it is tied to Document DB cost spike investigation and prevention activity86d1nmbdh

name: Forge fixes - ArgoCD, Secrets and other issues

comments.text:
ArgoCD Slow Sync Issue
The ArgoCD Application Controller is frequently getting OOMKilled, which is causing major performance issues. Kubernetes terminates the controller whenever it exceeds its memory limit, leading to repeated interruptions in sync operations.
Evidence
Current State:
Total applications: 1,219 (very high for a single controller)
Controller memory usage: 8.28 GB out of a 12 GB limit (continuously increasing)
CPU usage: 2.3 cores (high)
Restart count: 15 restarts in the last 8 days (about two restarts per day)
OOMKill Details:

Last State:     Terminated
Reason:         OOMKilled
Exit Code:      137
Started:        Wed, 03 Dec 2025 23:53:33 +0530
Finished:       Thu, 04 Dec 2025 12:52:21 +0530
Restart Count:  15
Exit code 137 confirms the controller was killed due to memory exhaustion.
Last Termination Event:

{
  "terminated": {
    "exitCode": 137,
    "finishedAt": "2025-12-04T07:22:21Z",
    "reason": "OOMKilled",
    "startedAt": "2025-12-03T18:23:33Z"
  }
}
The controller typically runs for around 13 hours before being killed, and this cycle repeats consistently.

When the controller is OOMKilled, all sync operations stop immediately.
After restarting, it must reconcile all 1,219 applications from scratch.
Heavy memory usage slows reconciliation even before the crash.
This cycle repeats every 12–13 hours, causing repeated sync delays of 30 minutes or more.

ExternalSecrets were configured with a PreSync hook, causing them to be deleted and reapplied during every sync. If any PreSync job (e.g., DB migration) failed, the    ExternalSecret would still get deleted as part of the PreSync phase. example i had shared in below failed db migrationjob job pic(userxp-5 namespace)
Fix:
Removed ExternalSecrets from the PreSync hook so they are now applied as part of a normal sync with -100 sync wave, preventing unintended deletion
Added conditional logic (if/else) so the change is applied only for QA.

comments.text:
@Souraj Chakraborty  @Karthik 

This EC2 instance is part of a Kubernetes node hosting a legitimate internal service (Cost Guardian) that retrieves AWS cost and usage data by making AWS API calls. Under normal conditions, DNS resolution is handled via the VPC’s default Amazon-provided DNS.
However, during periods where AWS API calls intermittently fail or experience DNS resolution issues, the application’s DNS resolution fallback mechanism temporarily routes DNS queries to Google Public DNS (8.8.4.4) to ensure service continuity and prevent request failures.
As a result, outbound DNS traffic to a non-default resolver was observed, which triggered the GuardDuty DefenseEvasion:EC2/UnusualDNSResolver alert.

Impact:
The behavior is expected and legitimate for this workload.
No indicators of compromise or malicious activity were identified.
The traffic originated from a known Kubernetes service with a valid business purpose.

after the holidays. Here's what really happened: Throughout October, November, and December 2025, our load balancer 
was handling about 14-15 million requests per day during weekdays, which is our normal business traffic. Then during
the holidays (December 24th through January 4th), traffic dropped way down to around 8 million requests per day 
because people weren't working and using our applications as much. When everyone came back to work on January 5th, 
traffic immediately jumped back up to the normal 15 million requests per day - the same levels we had before the 
holidays.

name: fluentd pod is in pending state - hiverhq-backend cluster

comments.text:
1. What happened
One Fluentd DaemonSet pod stayed Pending with:
0/23 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 22 node(s) didn't satisfy plugin(s) [NodeAffinity].
The “1 node” is ip-172-30-49-1 (prometheus node group). The DaemonSet runs one pod per node, so that pod must schedule on this node. The node had ~105m CPU free (by requests) while Fluentd was asking for 300m → scheduler could not place it.

2. Why this node is different (load not equally distributed)
All three nodes are in the same prometheus-nodes group (t3a.xlarge, ~3920m allocatable CPU):


undefinedSo:
49-1 has almost all of the “stack” (Prometheus replica, Thanos components, Grafana) plus Fluentd.
16-200 has one Prometheus replica and a few components.
50-12 is underused: same capacity but no heavy monitoring workloads.
The other nodes don’t use less because they’re more efficient; fewer heavy pods were scheduled there. There is no pod anti-affinity (or similar) to spread the stack across the three nodes, so the scheduler placed most of it on 49-1.

3. Short-term fix (already done)
Change: Fluentd DaemonSet CPU request reduced from 300m → 100m (limits unchanged: 1500m CPU, 1500Mi memory).
Result: Fluentd pod could schedule on 49-1 (~105m free); all Fluentd pods are now running.
Revert if needed:
kubectl patch daemonset fluentd-backend -n kube-system --type='json' -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources/requests/cpu", "value": "300m"}]'
This is a short-term fix: it fixes the immediate “Fluentd pending” issue but does not fix the underlying imbalance.

4. Long-term: equalising load across the prometheus nodes
Goals
Spread Prometheus/Thanos/Grafana so no single node is at 97% requested CPU.
Use 50-12 (and 16-200) more and avoid overloading 49-1.
Reduce risk of future “Insufficient cpu” on 49-1 when new DaemonSets or other workloads are added.
Recommendations
Add pod anti-affinity to the monitoring stack
For Prometheus, Thanos (query, compactor, query-frontend, bucketweb), and Grafana:
Prefer spreading across nodes, e.g. podAntiAffinity with topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname (and optionally topology.kubernetes.io/zone for AZ spread).
This will push new/rolling pods onto 16-200 and 50-12 instead of piling on 49-1.
Re-balance existing workloads
Option A: Restart or delete some of the heavy pods on 49-1 (e.g. Thanos query, compactor, Grafana) so they reschedule; with anti-affinity in place, they should land on 16-200 or 50-12.
Option B: Temporarily scale down/up or adjust replicas so the scheduler places new pods on the less loaded nodes, then add anti-affinity so future rollouts stay spread.
Review and adjust resource requests
Ensure Prometheus/Thanos/Grafana requests are realistic (not over-requesting). Right-sizing can free headroom on 49-1 and make scheduling more predictable.
Optional: dedicate a node to “heavy” monitoring
If you prefer to keep the stack on one node, consider a larger instance for that node (or a dedicated node pool) so Fluentd + system DaemonSets can always schedule there without reducing Fluentd’s request as a workaround.
Track and alert
Use existing monitoring (e.g. Datadog/Prometheus) to alert when a node’s requested CPU (or utilisation) goes above a threshold (e.g. 85–90%) so you can rebalance or scale before pods go Pending.

Note :- Why didn't we receive the pod pending status alert ?

name: Feature-flag-daemon deployement in omni, and doing the redis configuration
description:
related omni clickup → 

Context:
Omni is integrating with the Feature Flag functionality.
The Feature Flag service uses a Redis instance:
feature-flag-sdk-redis.qaensh.ng.0001.usw2.cache.amazonaws.com
This Redis is currently deployed inside the HIG VPC.

Problem:
Omni pods are running in a different VPC, and therefore:
They cannot directly access the Redis instance in HIG VPC.
Because of this, Omni cannot fetch or evaluate feature flags.

Devops:
We see two possible approaches:
Option 1: VPC Peering 

Establish VPC Peering between Omni VPC and HIG VPC
Option 2: Deploy Feature-Flag Daemon in Omni

Deploy a feature-flag-daemon inside Omni VPC

comments.text: @Rohit kumar Update: We have implemented Option 1, which is the most straightforward and direct approach to release this feature with minimal risk. Please let me know if anything is pending from my side.

Hi @Tanish Jain, @Gaurav Chaudhary 
For a longer run we can consider the below Option. 

Use AWS PrivateLink for Service-Level Connectivity: 
As an alternative to full VPC peering, we can use AWS PrivateLink to provide secure, service-level connectivity between the Omni and HIG environments.
Approach
Expose the required service (e.g., Redis or feature-flag service) from the HIG VPC as a PrivateLink endpoint service.
Create an interface endpoint in the Omni VPC that connects only to this specific service.
Restrict access to the endpoint using security groups and least-privilege rules.
Key Benefits
Avoids full VPC-to-VPC network trust, reducing the attack surface.
Exposes only the required service instead of the entire VPC.
Provides stronger network isolation and better security posture.
Easier to audit and control compared to traditional VPC peering.
Security Advantages
No lateral movement risk across VPCs.
Fine-grained access control at the service level.
Aligns better with least-privilege and zero-trust architecture principles.
Considerations
Slightly higher setup complexity compared to VPC peering.
Additional per-endpoint AWS cost, though typically lower than the cost of enabling full VPC flow logs.
PrivateLink reduces the network trust boundary from VPC-level to service-level, which is a major security improvement.

Thanks

HI @Tanish Jain, @Rohit kumar, 
As per our discussion we suggest you to proceed with Option 2. But if you want to proceed with Option 1 due to less bandwidth then please follow the below Recommended Controls. 

Enable Encryption must in transit & Rest. 
Security group rule allow only to the source 172.**.*.*/16 and the port is 6378. No broad CIDR access.
Enable VPC flow logs for the peering subnets and Create Redis connection spike alerts
Note:- RDS and other sensitive systems remain blocked

As a longer-term improvement, enabling Redis authentication or moving to a more isolated connectivity model can be considered (Option 2).

Please proceed with the change while ensuring the above controls remain in place.

CC: @Gaurav Chaudhary

Hi @Karthik 
 Omni is integrating with the Feature Flag functionality, which depends on a Redis instance:
feature-flag-sdk-redis.qaensh.ng.0001.usw2.cache.amazonaws.com

This Redis is currently deployed inside the HIG VPC, while Omni pods are running in a different VPC (HOT). Because of this network separation:
Omni pods cannot directly access the Redis instance in HIG.
As a result, Omni cannot fetch or evaluate feature flags, which blocks the integration.

The requirement is to access HGT Redis from the HOT EKS cluster. To enable this securely and reliably, we plan to set up VPC peering between HOT and HGT and allow connectivity only to the HGT ElastiCache endpoint.
I discussed this with @Harshit Mittal  and he is aligned with this approach. Since ElastiCache is used as a caching / ephemeral data store and does not contain persistent or system-of-record data we believe this change is acceptable from a risk perspective.

Please note that RDS endpoints will remain blocked, as they contain critical and sensitive data.
Do you see any concerns or risks before we proceed with these changes?

name: guardduty cost spike investigation

comments.text: repost.aws/knowledge-center/monthly-aws-billing

The cost spike on the 1st of every month is caused by AWS finalizing the previous month’s billing, not by sudden new usage.
Your main cost drivers are:
USW2-PaidEventsAnalyzed-Bytes (~50%)
USW2-PaidKubernetesAuditLogsAnalyzed (~23%)
Additional portions from EventsAnalyzed and S3DataEvents
These charges come from GuardDuty analyzing:
VPC Flow Logs
CloudTrail events
EKS Kubernetes audit logs
S3 data events
Throughout the month, charges are shown as estimates. At the beginning of the new month, AWS finalizes and reconciles billing, which can cause larger amounts to appear on Day 1.
As stated on AWS re:Post:
“AWS finalizes your monthly AWS bill at the start of the new month… typically between the first and fifth day of the month.”
Therefore, the spike on the 1st is month-end billing reconciliation, not a sudden increase in usage.

There is a recurring pattern of increased GuardDuty costs during the first week of every month.
The spike is primarily driven by higher usage in:
USW2-PaidEventsAnalyzed-Bytes
USW2-PaidKubernetesAuditLogsAnalyzed
Based on historical trends, this appears to be a consistent monthly pattern rather than an anomaly.

name: p0- Increase Buffer storage of elasticsearch nodes
description:
Issue Description
We have been facing a persistent Elasticsearch–Fluentd buffer size ratio increase for the past several months, and it has now become a major operational pain point.
This issue has led to frequent Fluentd and Elasticsearch alerts, increased operational overhead, and periodic instability in the logging pipeline.
Impact
Continuous alerting from Fluentd buffer growth and Elasticsearch disk usage
Risk of index write blocks when nodes approach high disk utilization
Reduced reliability of log ingestion and delayed indexing
Increased on-call and manual intervention effort

Investigations & Mitigations Attempted
We have already explored and implemented multiple mitigation strategies, including:
Shard relocation across Elasticsearch nodes
Index and data cleanup
Leveraging QuotaKeeper to control log ingestion rates
Fluentd restarts and tuning
While these steps provided temporary relief, they did not resolve the underlying issue.

Observations
Log ingestion volume has significantly increased due to onboarding of new services
Elasticsearch storage usage has grown substantially
The underlying storage bucket size increased from ~80 TB to ~125 TB, indicating a sustained rise in log data being pushed into Elasticsearch
Current node storage capacity is no longer sufficient to handle the increased ingestion rate

Root Cause (Likely)
The existing Elasticsearch node storage capacity is undersized for the current and growing log ingestion volume, causing frequent buffer backlogs and disk pressure.

Proposed Solution
To restore stability and provide headroom for current and future growth, we propose to:
Increase Elasticsearch node storage by 400 GiB per node
This will:
Reduce disk pressure
Prevent frequent buffer backlogs
Improve overall cluster stability
Minimize operational intervention and alert noise

name: Investigating notes DB restart on 04th Feb, 2026
description:
Notes Db restarted last week on 4th Feb


Need to investigate why this happened - Is it a planned activity from AWS end, or it happened because of unhealthy DB ?

comments.text:
@Karun Kumar Acknowledged, and agreed — this should be treated as a process failure, independent of customer impact.

Sharing the RCA based on investigation and discussion with @Akash Yadav 
Root Cause Analysis - RDS Instance Restart

Issue: Two RDS instances restarted unexpectedly after enabling automated backups.
Root Cause: While enabling automated backups typically does NOT require a restart in AWS RDS, there is a critical blind spot specific to MySQL and MariaDB engines: changing the backup retention period from 0 (disabled) to any positive value triggers a mandatory restart.
Technical Explanation:
General Case: Enabling or modifying automated backups does not require a restart
MySQL/MariaDB Exception: When backup retention changes from 0 to >0, AWS RDS must enable binary logging infrastructure for point-in-time recovery support
Binary logging is a core database engine feature that can only be activated through a database restart
This is a one-time occurrence during initial backup enablement only
Blind Spot Identified: The restart requirement for MySQL/MariaDB when transitioning from no backups (retention = 0) to enabled backups (retention > 0) is not widely understood and differs from other RDS engines and general backup modification scenarios.

We’ll ensure stronger change controls going forward, including double-checking configurations, validating assumptions, and coordinating upfront, so such scenarios do not recur.

name: Temporary DB connection from OMNI BE to AI Automations database
description:
Context: We need to migrate old customers from Automation1.0 to Automations2.0. As Automations2.0 is driven by AI Automation service, we would need to migrate the automation records that are already created for these customers. 
 
Precedence: 
When the migration was done in HIG, a script was ran which took the old automation records, transformed them and then inserted into the AI automations database. Ref script -   

Details of OMNI migration are mentioned in this doc -  

At a high level there are 2 components.
Transforming current automation records to the tree based structure that AI automation service expects.
Saving the transformed records.

Following are different approaches that we can take to complete the migration. Adding them below:
Kafka
Omni pushes events to kafka. Automation service consumes and creates records
Extra effort needed from Automation service: 2 days (infra setup, testing)
DB Dump
We create a DB dump of the Automation record creation and directly run on the AI automation table
No extra effort needed from Automation service except for some support. 
But this will not give any control over the migration activity - partial or full failures for particular account, etc.
Using CRUD
The admin-panel FE makes CRUD to AI automation service via heimdall authentication. These APIs can't be used by OMNI BE (confirmed by Sachin). 
Extra effort needed from Automation service: 1.5 days (new temporary API creation without Auth for OMNI BE)
Migration script
via the DB connection, insertion will be done by the migration script running in OMNI BE.
No extra effort needed from Automation service except for some support.
Gives control over the migration, we can skip failed accounts, we can run in small batches, we can control the qps, etc.

The 4th approach(migration script) is low effort and possible to conclude by this Saturday. Hence taking this ahead.


Database access required: automation_ai

The bug is in the Chrome extension generation workflow. When multiple areas (e.g., eagles-1 and eagles-2) are processed together, they all use the same working directory, which causes configuration leakage.
What’s happening
The base extension is downloaded once and unzipped into chrome_extension/.
The workflow then loops through multiple areas using this same directory.
For the first area (eagles-1), all <APP_ENV> placeholders are replaced with eagles-1.
For the next area (eagles-2), the workflow attempts to replace <APP_ENV> again, but the placeholders no longer exist.

For production fixes, we were facing similar resource constraints, so we split the workflow into two parts. 

One part runs on GitHub-hosted runners, while the other runs on our self-hosted runners.
Additionally, we have pushed the production images to our QA ECR to perform sanity testing before proceeding with the production release, as part of the new workflow.

Future action item: We have a limited quota for GitHub-hosted runners, so as a planned improvement, we will migrate the first workflow to self-hosted runners as well.

@Swetha Reddy Salkuti For now, please perform thorough sanity testing on the prod-build images and verify everything carefully before proceeding with the production release.
Prod-build - github.com/GrexIt/hiver-chatwoot/pull/111/changes#diff-26ca3cde615d742660661bee85b1fc68706164ab3fa149d5256d3cd8e67095ce

Root cause:
Asset precompile (rake assets:precompile) was running inside Docker on the self-hosted runner. It’s heavy (Node + Rails, ~50+ min, high memory) and was overloading the runner, leading to “runner lost communication” and failed builds.
Fix:Precompile assets on a GitHub-hosted runner (more RAM, stable), then upload public/assets as an artifact.
Build the image on the self-hosted runner after downloading that artifact and passing SKIP_ASSET_PRECOMPILE=1 so the Docker build does not run asset precompile and uses the prebuilt assets instead.
So: no change to application source code (Rails, Node, gems, JS). Only CI workflow and Dockerfile were changed.

name: OpenVpn CORS Issue

comments.text:
Summary of Fix & Current Status
The AWS SSO access issue observed in Chromium-based browsers has been provisionally resolved on the test machine. A temporary workaround has been applied as outlined below.
Temporary Fix Applied:
Disable the Local Network Access Checks flag in Chrome:
chrome://flags/#local-network-access-check

Root Cause 
Based on input from the OpenVPN team, the issue appears to be related to Chrome’s Private Network Access (PNA) security feature (now referred to as Local Network Access Checks). This feature can block or interfere with cross-origin requests from public to private networks when the required CORS headers are not present, leading to the observed authentication failures.

This issue is currently resolved via a workaround, however the root cause is still unknown.
 I’m actively coordinating with OpenVPN support, and they’ve asked us to reproduce the issue and share the HAR file for further analysis.
 To ensure this doesn’t get missed, I’m keeping the task in Tracking state and moving it to the next sprint until we get a permanent fix.

comments.text:
After a discussion with @Tanish Jain and @Karthik on this Task, it will not feasible for us to implement this as this can cause operational risks.

Given these constraints, we collectively agree that this requirement cannot be implemented safely using native GCP capabilities without introducing significant risk.

Resolution Summary – Feasibility Review of GCP Budget-Based Service Restriction
After reviewing GCP Organization Policy documentation, current org policy setup, and billing capabilities, the following limitations were identified:
Billing data is not real-time
GCP billing updates are delayed (typically up to 24 hours).
This makes real-time enforcement based on spend impossible, as actions will always be reactive and late.
GCP does NOT support dynamic service blocking based on spend
There is no native mechanism to:
Track per-service spend in real time.
Automatically disable only the service that crossed a specific cost threshold (₹3k–₹4k).
Budgets work only at project / billing account level, not at individual service enforcement level.
Cannot identify which service caused budget exhaustion
At the time of alert trigger, GCP does not reliably provide:
Exact service-level attribution required for targeted enforcement.
Organization Policies cannot enforce cost-based controls
Org policies are preventive governance controls, not billing-driven enforcement mechanisms.
They work on:
Service enable/disable rules
Resource constraints
Security and compliance guardrails
They cannot act dynamically based on spend thresholds.
Blocking resources instead of services is not practical
Resource-based deny policies would require:
Maintaining and managing 1600+ service APIs and resource types.
Continuous updates as GCP adds new services.
This is operationally unscalable, error-prone, and high-risk.
Service disablement is a hard stop
Disabling APIs can immediately break running applications and pipelines.
No throttling or soft-limit enforcement is supported.
Final Conclusion
Dynamic service restriction based on cost thresholds is NOT supported in GCP.
Organization Policies cannot fulfill this requirement, as they are not integrated with billing triggers or per-service cost enforcement.
The requirement is technically not feasible using native GCP capabilities.

Due to GCP platform limitations (project-level budgets, non-real-time alerts, no per-service cost enforcement), implementing this requirement exactly as defined is not feasible. Any solution would require trade-offs.

Given this, we can close this item.
CC: @Harshit Mittal

After evaluating the requirements against GCP capabilities, there are platform limitations that prevent implementing this exactly as defined:
GCP budgets work at the project/billing level, not at individual service spend level, so per-service cost blocking is not possible.
Budget alerts are not real-time, making enforcement best-effort with possible additional spend.
GCP does not expose which service caused the budget exhaustion, so targeting a specific service is unreliable.
Service disablement is a hard stop, not throttling, and can immediately impact workloads.
Disabling services does not guarantee zero cost due to existing resources (storage, disks, IPs).
GCP does not natively re-enable services on budget reset; monthly reset requires custom automation.
Conclusion: The original requirement assumes real-time, per-service cost enforcement, which is not supported by GCP without accepting trade-offs.

Clarification on GCP Service Restriction at ₹3k–₹4k Spend

 Around restricting services based on spend, a quick clarification on GCP limitations:
GCP does not support service-level cost enforcement.
It’s not possible to automatically block a specific GCP service (approved or non-approved) when that service alone crosses a ₹3k–₹4k spend.
GCP Budgets work at the project or billing account level, not at an individual service level.
Service-level billing data is not real-time and comes with delays, so enforcing actions based on live ₹ spend isn’t feasible.
What is possible:
Budget thresholds (₹3k–₹4k) can be configured for alerts only.
Hard enforcement (like disabling APIs) can be applied only when the overall project budget hits 100%.
At that stage, non-approved services can be automatically disabled, while approved services remain unaffected.
Recommendation:
Avoid auto-blocking approved services based purely on spend.
Use ₹3k–₹4k thresholds as early warning alerts.
Apply enforcement only for non-approved services after full budget exhaustion.
This approach aligns with GCP’s technical constraints, is safe for production, and can be fully automated.
